overview: You've probably heard the term insulin resistance before. Maybe your healthcare provider mentioned it. Maybe you've seen it on social media. Maybe you've heard that it's why people struggle with weight gain or why Type 2 diabetes develops.
But what exactly is insulin resistance? And more importantly, how would you know if you have it?

The truth is, insulin resistance doesn't usually appear overnight. It develops gradually, often over many years, and many people experience symptoms long before they're diagnosed with prediabetes or Type 2 diabetes. Recognizing those early signs gives you the opportunity to make changes before more serious health problems develop.

sections.title: What Is Insulin?
body: Every time you eat, your digestive system breaks food down into nutrients your body can use for energy. Carbohydrates are broken down into glucose (blood sugar), which becomes one of your body's primary fuel sources.
But glucose can't enter your cells by itself. That's where insulin comes in.

Insulin is a hormone made by your pancreas. Think of it as a key that unlocks your cells, allowing glucose to move from your bloodstream into your muscles, organs, and other tissues where it can be used for energy. When everything is working well, this process happens efficiently and your blood sugar stays within a healthy range.

image.alt: Illustration of insulin as a golden key unlocking a cell so glucose can enter

sections.title: What Is Insulin Resistance?
body: Over time, your cells can become less responsive to insulin. Imagine that key trying to unlock a door that has become sticky. The key still fits — it just doesn't work as well.

To overcome this, your pancreas produces more insulin to keep your blood sugar under control. For a while, it succeeds. That's why many people with insulin resistance still have normal blood sugar levels: their body is simply working much harder than it should.

Eventually, if insulin resistance continues to worsen, the pancreas may no longer be able to keep up. Blood sugar begins to rise, increasing the risk of prediabetes and, eventually, Type 2 diabetes. Insulin resistance is one of the earliest stages in that process.
sections.callout: Did you know? Many people with insulin resistance have completely normal fasting glucose levels. That's because the pancreas often produces extra insulin for years before blood sugar begins to rise. Looking at your health as a whole — including your history, body composition, lifestyle, and, when appropriate, additional laboratory markers — can provide a more complete picture of your metabolic health.

sections.title: What Are the Signs and Symptoms of Insulin Resistance?

body: Difficulty losing weight despite eating well
Weight gain around the abdomen or waistline
Craving sweets or carbohydrates
Feeling hungry again shortly after eating

items.label: Energy levels
body: Afternoon energy crashes
Feeling sleepy after meals
Fatigue despite getting adequate sleep
Brain fog or difficulty concentrating

items.label: Clinical markers
body: Increased waist circumference
Elevated blood pressure
High triglycerides
Low HDL ("good") cholesterol
Elevated fasting insulin levels

items.label: Physical & medical signs
body: Skin tags, especially around the neck or underarms
Dark, velvety skin around the neck, armpits, or groin (called acanthosis nigricans)
Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS), formerly PCOS
Fatty liver disease
A family history of Type 2 diabetes

closing: Having one or two of these doesn't necessarily mean you have insulin resistance — many of these symptoms can have other causes. But if several of them sound familiar, it's worth having a conversation with your healthcare provider.

sections.title: Why Does Insulin Resistance Matter?

Insulin resistance has been associated with an increased risk of:

items.label: Heart disease and high blood pressure
Fatty liver disease and metabolic syndrome

overview: Your hormones were never meant to stay the same. Understanding how they change, decade by decade, can help you navigate what comes next. At Arc Wellness in St. Louis, this is one of the questions our physician-led team hears most often, from patients in their 30s all the way through their 70s.
There is a strange expectation we place on our bodies: we expect them to function at 45 exactly the way they did at 25.

We expect the same energy. The same sleep. The same metabolism. The same strength. The same ability to recover after a long week, a hard workout, or a late night. And when something begins to change, we often assume we're doing something wrong.

Maybe the weight starts settling differently. Sleep becomes lighter. Muscle is harder to maintain. Your mood feels less predictable. Sexual desire changes, or your energy just isn't quite what it used to be.

For **women**, periods may begin changing long before menopause arrives. For **men**, the changes can be quieter, a gradual shift in testosterone, strength, recovery, body composition, or sexual function over many years.
Somewhere in the middle of all of this, people often say the exact same thing: "I just don't feel like myself anymore."
But perhaps a better question is: what does your body need in this decade?
article.overviewCallout: What does your body need in this decade?

sections.title: Your 30s: Building the Foundation
body: For many people, their 30s still feel relatively familiar. But beneath the surface, this is an incredibly important decade.
Careers are growing. Families are being built. Sleep may be sacrificed. Stress is often high, and exercise and nutrition can easily become whatever fits into an increasingly crowded schedule.

For **women**, hormonal patterns may begin to shift toward the latter part of this decade, although there is enormous individual variation. Fertility also changes with age, and subtle changes in cycles can sometimes be among the first signs that the hormonal landscape is evolving.

**Men** may not notice a dramatic hormonal transition, either. Testosterone levels generally change gradually with age, and sleep, excess body fat, certain medications, metabolic health, and other medical conditions can also influence testosterone and how someone feels.
This is why we think of your 30s less as a decade of correction and more as a decade of foundation. The habits built here can influence how you enter every decade that follows.
Focus on the Foundation:

image.alt: Inclusive diagram of a man and woman with sleep, strength, energy, and mood across the decades — hormone health as whole-person care

items.label: Pay attention to changes rather than waiting for them to become problems

sections.title: Your 40s: When the Signals Often Get Louder
body: For many **women**, the 40s are when the hormonal conversation becomes much more noticeable. Perimenopause can begin years before the final menstrual period, and it doesn't always announce itself with classic hot flashes.
Often, it looks like:

image.alt: Man and woman awake at night in midlife — quiet restlessness that can affect both

items.label: The sudden realization that the things you've always done to maintain your weight simply aren't working anymore

closing: **Men** experience their own midlife changes, although typically without the distinct, rapid hormonal transition that **women** experience with menopause. Changes in testosterone can occur gradually and may overlap with changes in sleep, [metabolic health](/treatments/metabolic-health), stress, medications, and lifestyle. Some **men** notice reduced energy, declining strength, changes in sexual function, or more difficulty maintaining lean muscle.
The takeaway: the important part is not to assume every midlife symptom is hormonal. But it's equally important not to assume that hormones don't matter. Context is everything.

sections.title: Your 50s: The Conversation Shifts from Symptoms to Longevity
body: For many **women**, the 50s include the transition into menopause. But menopause is not simply the end of menstrual cycles. Estrogen influences tissues throughout the body, which is one reason the conversation at this stage deserves to be broader than hot flashes alone.

For **men**, this decade can also bring more noticeable changes in strength, body composition, energy, or sexual health. When symptoms suggest a hormonal issue, evaluation should look at the whole person rather than treating a testosterone number in isolation.
This is the decade when we want to think increasingly about what we're preserving. Not just how you feel today, but asking the right questions for tomorrow:

items.label: How strong do we want you to be at 70?
How do we protect your bone density?
How do we maintain your muscle mass?
How do we support cardiovascular and metabolic health?
How do we keep you engaged, capable, and independent?

closing: At this stage, hormonal health becomes part of a much larger longevity conversation.

sections.title: Your 60s, 70s & Beyond: Protecting What Keeps You Living Well
body: Eventually, the question changes again. It becomes less about trying to feel the way you did when you were younger and much more about protecting the things that allow you to live the way you want to live.
The Pillars of Independence:

image.alt: Man and woman walking outdoors — strength and mobility supporting independence with age

closing: Hormones remain one piece of that picture, but they are never the entire picture. Nutrition matters. Movement matters. Muscle matters tremendously. Sleep, connection, purpose, and preventive healthcare matter.
Medical decisions, including whether hormone therapy is appropriate, become increasingly individualized based on symptoms, health history, risks, goals, and stage of life.
Because longevity isn't simply about adding years. It's about protecting the life inside those years.

sections.title: Hormone Care Shouldn't Begin and End With a Number
body: This is where hormone conversations can become too simple: low number? Replace it. Normal number? Ignore it.
But bodies aren't quite that tidy. A thoughtful hormone evaluation starts with the person, not the lab slip.
The questions we need to ask:

items.label: What has changed, and when did it change?
What has happened to your strength and body composition?
What does your metabolic health look like?

closing: Then, we decide whether testing makes sense, and what those results actually mean in context.

Sometimes [hormone therapy](/treatments/hormone-health) may be appropriate. Sometimes another issue needs attention first. Sometimes lifestyle changes can have a meaningful impact. And sometimes what you're experiencing is a normal transition that simply deserves better support and understanding.
The goal isn't to chase youth. It's to support health through change.

title: Inflammation: Your Body's Built-In Alarm System
excerpt: When it protects you, and when it starts working against you.
imageAlt: Editorial medical illustration of a gender-neutral human figure with warm glow points at joints and abdomen — chronic inflammation across the body
body: Inflammation has become one of the biggest buzzwords in modern healthcare. It's blamed for fatigue, weight gain, joint pain, brain fog, heart disease, autoimmune conditions, aging, and even wrinkles.

Wander down any grocery store aisle, and you will find shelves lined with products proudly claiming to be "anti-inflammatory." A quick scroll through social media makes it sound as though all inflammation is a toxic enemy you must vanquish.
But the truth is much more interesting.
Inflammation isn't your enemy. In fact, it's one of the most important ways your body protects you. The problem is when it never gets the chance to turn off.
The Biological First Responder
Your body was entirely designed to create inflammation.

Imagine you accidentally cut your finger while cooking dinner. Within seconds, your body begins responding. Blood vessels change. Specialized immune cells arrive. Chemical messengers signal that help is on the way. The area becomes red, warm, swollen, and tender.
That's inflammation.

And in this situation, it is exactly what you want. Without it, wounds wouldn't heal, simple infections would spread rapidly, and your body would struggle to repair itself. Inflammation is your body's natural, essential repair system.
When the Alarm Never Shuts Off

Now, imagine your home's smoke alarm. When there's a real fire, you want it to sound. It saves lives. But if that alarm continued blaring for weeks after the fire was out, it would stop protecting you and start disrupting your life.
The exact same thing happens inside your body.
Sometimes the inflammatory response continues long after it has served its vital purpose. Instead of helping the body heal, this ongoing inflammation begins affecting how your body functions.

Acute Inflammation (The Helper): Purpose — Protects and heals the body; Trigger — Direct injury, cut, or acute infection; Duration — Short-term (days to weeks); Symptoms — Localized redness, heat, swelling, pain

Chronic Inflammation (The Disruptor): Purpose — Harms healthy tissues over time; Trigger — Chronic stress, poor diet, lifestyle factors; Duration — Long-term (months to years); Symptoms — Systemic fatigue, brain fog, stealthy changes
The Quiet Threat: What Does Chronic Inflammation Feel Like?

Unlike a cut or an infection, chronic inflammation is often incredibly quiet. Most people don't wake up and "feel inflamed." Instead, they notice subtle, frustrating changes that develop gradually over time.
You may experience:
Persistent fatigue
Brain fog or difficulty concentrating
Achy joints or muscles
Slower recovery after exercise
Chronically low energy
Poor sleep
Increased abdominal weight gain
Frequent illness
Skin changes or breakouts
Digestive complaints

These symptoms are not specific to inflammation alone, many different medical conditions can cause them. But when several occur together, they are clear clues that your overall health deserves a closer look.
What is Triggering the Alarm?
There is rarely one single cause for chronic inflammation. It is a highly complex response influenced by many aspects of our daily lives, including:
Poor sleep
Chronic stress
Smoking or vaping
Excess visceral (abdominal) body fat
Diets high in ultra-processed foods
Physical inactivity
Poor metabolic health
Autoimmune diseases
Certain infections
Environmental exposures
Untreated chronic medical conditions

Genetics also play a role. Some people are simply more susceptible than others. This is precisely why inflammation isn't something we can "treat" with one magical supplement or a single superfood. We have to work to understand why the body is generating that response in the first place.
The Bigger Picture: Beyond Sore Joints

When inflammation remains elevated over time, it casts a shadow over multiple body systems. Researchers continue to study its driving role in serious conditions such as cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, fatty liver disease, arthritis, autoimmune conditions, neurodegenerative diseases, and some cancers.
Inflammation doesn't necessarily cause these conditions all by itself, but it is one critical piece of a much larger puzzle.
Can You Measure Inflammation?
Sometimes. Healthcare providers may use laboratory markers such as C-reactive protein (CRP) or other tests when clinically appropriate.

These markers can provide highly useful information, but they don't tell the entire story. A laboratory result is just one data point. Your symptoms, medical history, nutrition, sleep quality, stress levels, physical activity, and metabolic health all matter immensely. Numbers should always be interpreted in the context of your actual life.
Reducing chronic inflammation isn't about chasing a laboratory number. It's about supporting overall health.
Turning Down the Heat: Supporting Natural Balance
One of the most encouraging things about chronic inflammation is that the exact same habits that support a long, vibrant life also help support a healthy inflammatory response.
That includes:
Eating a diet rich in vegetables, fruits, legumes, nuts, healthy fats, and quality protein
Building and maintaining muscle through strength training
Walking and moving throughout the day
Prioritizing truly restorative sleep
Managing and mitigating chronic stress
Maintaining a healthy weight when appropriate
Avoiding tobacco products
Treating underlying medical conditions
Notice a trend? These aren't secret "anti-inflammatory tricks." They are simply the unshakeable foundations of good health.
Arc Wellness Perspective
At Arc Wellness, we don't believe inflammation is something to fear. We believe it's something to understand.

Your body isn't trying to work against you. More often than not, it's simply responding to something it perceives as a threat or a challenge. Our role is to step back, look at the whole picture, and ask better questions:
Why is your body responding this way?
Is there an underlying medical condition?
Could your nutrition, sleep, stress, hormones, or metabolic health be contributing?
What changes are likely to have the greatest impact, not just for today, but for the decades ahead?
Our goal isn't simply to quiet your symptoms. It's to help create an environment where your body can heal, recover, and function exactly the way it was beautifully designed to.
Understand what's behind your symptoms.
If you're in the St. Louis area, our physician-led team is here to help you look at the whole picture—not just a single lab marker.

Frequently Asked Questions
Is all inflammation bad?

No. Acute inflammation is a healthy, essential response that helps your body heal from injury and infection. It only becomes a concern when it turns chronic and continues long after the original trigger is gone.
How do I know if I have chronic inflammation?

Chronic inflammation often shows up as a cluster of subtle symptoms, persistent fatigue, brain fog, achy joints, poor sleep, or slower recovery, rather than one obvious sign. A physician-guided evaluation, sometimes including markers like CRP, combined with a look at your metabolic health and lifestyle, gives a clearer picture than any single lab number alone.
Can chronic inflammation be reversed?

In many cases, yes. Chronic inflammation often responds well to the same foundational habits that support overall health: better sleep, regular movement, a nutrient-dense diet, stress management, and treatment of any underlying medical conditions.

title: Is Your Gut Trying to Tell You Something?
titleLines: Is Your Gut Trying to Tell You Something?
Understanding the Everyday Signs of Digestive Imbalance
excerpt: Understanding the Everyday Signs of Digestive Imbalance
imageAlt: Teal and gold anatomical gut model on cream — an informative view of the digestive system
body: Your digestive system is remarkably good at getting your attention. Sometimes it's obvious—a stomach bug or a bout of food poisoning. But more often, the signs are subtle.

You feel bloated after meals. You battle constipation or frequent diarrhea. Certain foods suddenly don't agree with you, or you experience heartburn more often than you used to. You always seem to have "a sensitive stomach."
Over time, many people begin accepting these symptoms as normal: "I've always been this way." "It's just stress." "It's probably getting older."

But while digestive symptoms are common, they shouldn't simply be ignored. Your gut is one of the hardest-working systems in your body, and when something isn't functioning well, it often affects much more than digestion alone.
Your gut is one of the hardest-working systems in your body—and when something isn't functioning well, it often affects much more than digestion alone.
Your Gut Does Much More Than Digest Food
When most people think about digestive health, they think about the stomach. In reality, your gastrointestinal tract is responsible for far more than breaking down meals.

It even has a close relationship with your brain through what researchers call the [gut–brain axis](/treatments/gut-health). When your digestive system is functioning well, you rarely think about it. When it isn't, the effects can ripple throughout your entire body.
Nutrient absorption: It is the primary center where nutrients are absorbed.
Gut microbiome: It is home to trillions of bacteria that make up your gut microbiome.
Immune communication: It communicates constantly with your immune system.
Metabolism & vitamins: It influences how your body processes food, [regulates blood sugar](/treatments/metabolic-health), and produces certain vitamins.
Gut–brain axis: It has a close relationship with your brain through what researchers call the [gut–brain axis](/treatments/gut-health).
Common Signs Your Gut May Need Attention

Not every digestive symptom points to a serious condition. Many can be temporary and resolve on their own. But if symptoms become persistent, frequent, or begin affecting your quality of life, they deserve a closer look.
Sometimes people experience symptoms outside the digestive tract as well. While these symptoms can have many different causes, digestive health is one piece of the puzzle that may be worth exploring.

Non-digestive signs that may be worth exploring: Brain fog; Low energy; Iron deficiency or vitamin deficiencies; Skin changes; Difficulty maintaining a healthy weight; [Ongoing inflammation](/blogs/understanding-chronic-inflammation); Changes in mood

Common digestive signs: Frequent bloating; Constipation; Diarrhea; Alternating constipation and diarrhea; Excessive gas; Acid reflux or frequent heartburn; Stomach discomfort after eating; Feeling overly full after small meals; Food intolerances or increasing food sensitivities; Nausea; Abdominal pain or cramping; Unexplained fatigue after meals
The important point isn't to assume your gut is causing every symptom. It's to recognize that the body works as an interconnected system.
What Causes Digestive Problems?
There isn't one single answer. Digestive symptoms can result from many different conditions, including:
Diet and nutrition
Stress
Food intolerances
Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)
Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)
Celiac disease
Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis)
Gallbladder disease
Certain medications
Infections
Changes in the gut microbiome
Sometimes more than one factor is contributing at the same time. That's why simply treating a symptom on the surface doesn't always solve the underlying problem.
Your Gut and Your Brain Are Constantly Talking
Have you ever noticed your stomach "dropping" when you're nervous? Or lost your appetite during a stressful week? That's not your imagination.

The digestive system and the brain communicate continuously through the [gut–brain axis](/treatments/gut-health). Stress can change digestion. Poor digestion can affect how you feel. Sleep influences gut health. Gut health can influence sleep. One system affects the other.
Understanding those connections often helps explain why improving digestive health isn't always about one medication or one food. Sometimes it's about supporting the entire system.
Healing Doesn't Usually Happen Through a Cleanse

One of the biggest misconceptions about gut health is the idea that your digestive system simply needs to be "reset" with a harsh detox or cleanse. In reality, your gut is already remarkably good at maintaining itself.
What it often needs is consistency:
A diet rich in fiber
A variety of colorful fruits and vegetables
Beans and lentils
Whole grains
Healthy fats
Adequate hydration
Regular movement
Quality sleep
Stress management

Supporting your gut isn't about perfection. It's about creating an environment where it can function the way it was designed to—and when appropriate, identifying medical conditions that deserve proper treatment.
When Should You Talk to Your Healthcare Provider?

Digestive symptoms that are persistent, worsening, or interfering with daily life deserve medical evaluation. You should also seek immediate medical attention if you experience red-flag symptoms such as:
Blood in your stool
Unintentional weight loss
Persistent vomiting
Difficulty swallowing
Severe abdominal pain
Black or tar-colored stools
Symptoms that wake you from sleep regularly
These symptoms don't necessarily mean something serious is happening, but they should never be ignored.
The Arc Perspective
At Arc Wellness, we believe digestive health is about more than relieving symptoms. It's about understanding why those symptoms are happening in the first place.
Sometimes the answer is as simple as improving nutrition or increasing fiber. Sometimes stress, sleep, or medications are playing a larger role. Sometimes further medical evaluation is needed.

Our goal isn't to label every digestive complaint as "leaky gut" or assume every symptom comes from the microbiome. Our goal is to understand the whole picture—your symptoms, your history, your lifestyle, and your overall health—so we can help you make informed decisions about what comes next.
Because when your digestive system functions well, everything from your energy to your nutrition, [metabolism](/treatments/metabolic-health), and daily comfort can benefit.

What are the signs of poor gut health?

Gut imbalance often shows up as a cluster of everyday symptoms rather than one obvious sign—frequent bloating, constipation or diarrhea, heartburn, discomfort after eating, or increasing food sensitivities. Some people also notice symptoms outside the digestive tract, such as brain fog, low energy, or skin changes. When several occur together or become persistent, they deserve a closer look.
Can gut problems cause symptoms outside the stomach?

They can be connected. The body works as an interconnected system, and the gut communicates constantly with the immune system and the brain through the [gut–brain axis](/treatments/gut-health). While symptoms like fatigue, mood changes, or ongoing inflammation have many possible causes, digestive health is one piece of the puzzle worth exploring.
Do I need a cleanse or detox to reset my gut?

Usually not. Your gut is already remarkably good at maintaining itself, and a harsh cleanse isn't what it needs. More often it responds to consistency—fiber, colorful fruits and vegetables, whole grains, healthy fats, hydration, movement, quality sleep, and stress management.

title: Why You're Tired Even When Your Labs Are "Normal"
excerpt: When everything looks fine on paper, but you know something has changed.
imageAlt: Man sitting on the edge of his bed in morning light, dressed for the day but visibly drained — tired even when everything looks fine on paper
body: You're getting through the day. You're working, taking care of everyone, and keeping up with the things that need to be done. But somewhere along the way, your energy changed.

Maybe mornings are harder than they used to be, the afternoon slump has become an everyday occurrence, or you're relying on coffee more than you'd like. You might find that your workouts take more out of you, or your concentration isn't quite as sharp. Or maybe it's harder to explain than that. You just don't feel like yourself.

So, you have your labs checked. And the good news is, nothing concerning shows up. Your results are within range, and everything looks... normal. But you still feel tired. And that leaves an important question:
If nothing is "wrong," why don't I feel well?
The Space Between Illness and Optimal Health
There is a space between illness and feeling your best, and this is where we believe the conversation around health becomes much more interesting.

A normal laboratory result matters. Reference ranges help physicians recognize disease, identify abnormalities, and make important medical decisions. But your health is bigger than whether a collection of numbers has crossed a threshold.

Sometimes the earliest clues are much quieter. Your energy changes, your sleep becomes less restorative, and you don't recover the way you once did. Your body composition begins shifting despite doing the same things you've always done. Brain fog creeps in, and your motivation feels different. None of those things automatically mean something is wrong. But when you notice a change in how you feel or function, we believe it's worth asking why.
Energy Is Complex: Looking at the Patterns

The answer may not be one thing. Energy is surprisingly complex. It can be influenced by how well you're sleeping, how you're nourishing your body, your metabolic health, stress and recovery, medications, nutrient status, thyroid function, hormonal changes, inflammation, and underlying medical conditions.

And often, these things don't exist in neat little boxes. Poor sleep can affect glucose regulation, hormonal changes can affect sleep, and chronic stress can impact your appetite, recovery, and energy. Even changes in nutrition can influence iron or other nutrient levels. One shift can begin affecting another. That is why we look for patterns, not just isolated numbers.
Ferritin Level: Means more when we understand your iron history, nutrition, and symptoms.
Glucose Result: Means more when we can see how it has changed over several years.
Thyroid Marker: Means more in the context of your symptoms and previous results.
Hormones: Mean more when we consider your age, stage of life, sleep, body composition, sexual health, and how you actually feel.
The individual pieces matter, but the story they tell together matters more.
Your Body Evolves. Your Healthcare Should Too.

Your body changes through the decades, and your healthcare should be able to change with it. What your body needed at 30 may look very different at 45. And what supports you at 45 may change again at 60, 70, and beyond. Hormones shift, muscle mass changes, and metabolism evolves. Sleep can become different, nutritional needs change, while cardiovascular and cognitive health become increasingly important.

This doesn't mean every change should be treated, and it certainly doesn't mean aging is something that needs to be "fixed." It means we should understand what's changing so we can make thoughtful decisions about what deserves attention.

That's a very different approach from chasing symptoms. It's also why your trends over time can be so valuable. Instead of asking only, "Is this result normal?" we can also ask if this is normal for you. Has something been steadily changing? Does it correspond with the way you've been feeling? And does the bigger picture suggest that we should look a little closer?
Better Understanding, Not Just More Testing
More testing isn't the goal. Better understanding is. This distinction matters to us.

Comprehensive wellness shouldn't mean ordering every laboratory test available and searching until we find an abnormal number. Sometimes additional testing is appropriate, and sometimes it isn't. Sometimes the next step is improving sleep, increasing protein, rebuilding muscle, changing the way you're eating, addressing stress, or reviewing medications. Sometimes traditional medical treatment is exactly what is needed. And sometimes the right answer is simply to watch, support, and reassess.
The goal isn't to find something wrong with you; the goal is to understand your health well enough to make good decisions about what comes next.
This Is Where the Arc Begins

At Arc Wellness, we believe some of the most meaningful conversations in healthcare happen before a diagnosis. They happen when someone says: I'm functioning, but I don't feel as good as I used to. Something has changed. I want to understand my body better. I want to stay healthy as I get older.

Those conversations give us an opportunity to look at your health from more than one direction—bringing together traditional medicine, functional thinking, lifestyle, prevention, and longevity rather than asking you to choose between them.

Because the goal isn't simply to help you avoid disease. It's to help you understand what your body needs now, while keeping an eye on where you're going next—through your 30s, your 40s, your 50s, and the decades beyond.
Your numbers matter, but so does the person behind them.

If your labs are normal, that's good news. And if you still don't feel like yourself, the conversation doesn't necessarily have to end there. Sometimes your body is asking for a closer look. Sometimes it needs a different kind of support. And sometimes, what you need most is someone willing to put all the pieces together.
If you're tired and your labs look fine, let's look closer together.

title: Losing Weight… and Your Hair?
excerpt: What to Know About Hair Loss on a GLP-1
imageAlt: Woman looking in the mirror and parting her hair to check her scalp
body: You are losing the weight. Your clothes are fitting better. You are feeling better about yourself. Maybe you are finally seeing changes you have been working toward for years.
And then one fine day, you look down in the shower and think…
Why is there so much hair down there?

Then you notice it in your brush. On your shirt. On the bathroom counter. And suddenly, instead of celebrating your weight loss, you are standing in front of the mirror examining your hairline from six different angles.
Naturally, the GLP-1 gets blamed.

After all, hair loss has been reported with some [GLP-1](/treatments/medical-weight-loss) based weight-loss medications. But the story is a little more complicated than “I started a GLP-1 and it made my hair fall out.”

In many cases, the medication itself may not be the primary problem. Instead, the shedding appears to be associated with what is happening while you are losing weight — particularly when weight comes off quickly or when your nutritional intake drops significantly.
First, You Probably Aren't Going Bald
The type of hair loss commonly seen during significant or rapid weight loss is called telogen effluvium.
That sounds terribly dramatic. It usually isn't.
Your hair naturally cycles through different phases of growth, transition, rest, and shedding. Normally, those hairs aren't all operating on the same schedule, so you don't really notice the process.

But physical stressors including rapid weight loss, illness, surgery, major hormonal changes, significant calorie restriction, and nutritional deficiencies can cause a larger-than-normal number of hairs to enter the resting phase around the same time.
A few months later, those hairs begin to shed. And because they're doing it together, you notice.

Your body is remarkably good at deciding where its resources need to go. When energy or nutrients become limited, it prioritizes the things required to keep you alive and functioning: your heart, brain, organs, immune system, tissue repair, and metabolism.
Hair growth? Your body considers that optional.
I realize some of you strongly disagree with this classification. Unfortunately, your hair follicles did not get a vote.
Why Can This Happen During GLP-1 Weight Loss?
GLP-1–based medications can dramatically change appetite and food intake. For many people, that's part of why they work so well.
You're less hungry. You become full faster. Food noise decreases. Portions get smaller. All good things until less food accidentally becomes not enough nutrition.

Someone who previously ate 2,000 or more calories per day may suddenly find herself eating 900 or 1,000 without really trying. Protein intake may fall. Meals may get skipped. Foods that once sounded appealing may suddenly become difficult to finish.
Add rapid weight loss to that equation and the body can experience a significant physiologic change in a relatively short period of time.

Hormonal changes, [thyroid dysfunction](/blogs/hormones-through-the-decades-st-louis-mo), illness, stress, certain medications, and other medical conditions can also contribute to hair loss which is why we shouldn't automatically blame every loose strand on a GLP-1.
The Protein Conversation Matters
If you've been around Arc for any length of time, you probably knew this was coming. We need to talk about protein.

Hair is primarily composed of a protein called keratin. If you're consistently eating too little protein while losing weight, your body has to decide where the protein you are eating is most needed. And once again, your vital organs win over your ponytail.

Adequate protein during weight loss isn't important only because of your hair. It helps preserve lean muscle, supports recovery and immune function, improves satiety, and provides amino acids needed throughout the body.

This is one reason we don't want GLP-1 weight loss to become a contest to see how little you can eat. The goal isn't simply to make the number on the scale smaller. The goal is to lose weight while maintaining a strong, well-nourished body.
So, How Do We Minimize Hair Shedding?
The answer isn't a magical hair gummy. Sorry. It starts with making sure your body has what it needs.

Eat enough: Weight loss requires an energy deficit, but a larger deficit isn't automatically better. Extremely low intake and very rapid weight loss can place additional stress on the body. We want intentional weight loss, not accidental undernourishment.

Prioritize protein: Protein should have a place at every meal. If you're taking a GLP-1 and struggling to eat enough, the question shouldn't just be how many calories you ate — it should be whether you gave your body enough nutrition.

Don't forget micronutrients: Iron, vitamin D, zinc, B vitamins, vitamin C, copper, and other nutrients all play roles in normal hair growth. Food comes first. When deficiencies are suspected, [appropriate lab testing and targeted supplementation](/treatments/supplements) make much more sense than guessing.

Support the whole hair-building process: Vitamin C helps support collagen synthesis. Zinc and copper participate in normal tissue and follicle function. Essential fatty acids and amino acids also contribute to healthy skin and hair. Your hair would really prefer an actual meal.
When Does the Shedding Start?
Here is the frustrating part: hair operates on a delay.

Telogen effluvium often becomes noticeable two to three months after the event that triggered it. That means the shedding you notice today may reflect rapid weight loss, illness, stress, inadequate nutrition, or another change that happened weeks or months ago.

Once the underlying trigger is addressed, shedding generally begins to improve over the following months. Visible regrowth can take several months, and returning to your previous fullness may take six months or longer.
When Hair Loss Deserves a Closer Look
Not every case of hair loss during weight loss is telogen effluvium.

If your hair loss is severe, continues to worsen, persists beyond several months, occurs in patches, involves scalp irritation or scarring, or you notice other symptoms, it deserves further evaluation.

We may need to look beyond your medication and consider things like [thyroid function](/treatments/hormone-health), iron status, anemia, hormonal changes, autoimmune conditions, medications, chronic illness, or other nutritional deficiencies.
And if you already had thinning hair before beginning weight loss, the change in your body may simply make an underlying hair-loss condition more noticeable.
That's why the answer shouldn't automatically be “Stop the GLP-1.” Sometimes the better question is: “What does my body need while I'm losing weight?”
The Arc Wellness Approach
At [Arc Wellness](/about), we don't believe successful weight loss should be measured only by pounds lost. We care about what is happening to the whole person while those pounds are coming off.

Are you maintaining muscle? Are you eating enough protein? Are you getting adequate nutrients? How is your energy? How are you sleeping? Are your hormones and thyroid optimized? Are there deficiencies developing that we need to address? And yes… how is your hair?

GLP-1 medications can be incredibly useful tools, but medication is only one part of a [successful weight-loss program](/programs). Nutrition, strength, [metabolic health](/treatments/metabolic-health), appropriate supplementation, laboratory monitoring, and sustainable habits matter too.
Because losing weight shouldn't mean losing the things you wanted to keep. Especially your hair.
Frequently Asked Questions
Does a GLP-1 like semaglutide or tirzepatide directly cause hair loss?

Not usually in a direct way. Most GLP-1–related hair shedding is telogen effluvium, a temporary shedding pattern triggered by rapid weight loss and reduced nutritional intake rather than the medication itself.
What is telogen effluvium?

Telogen effluvium is a temporary, diffuse hair shedding that happens when a physical stressor such as rapid weight loss, illness, surgery, or nutritional deficiency pushes more hairs than normal into the resting (telogen) phase at the same time.
How much protein do I need on a GLP-1 to protect my hair?

Needs vary by person, but protein should be included at every meal from sources like eggs, fish, poultry, lean meats, beans, lentils, cottage cheese, Greek yogurt, and tofu. Arc Wellness can help calculate a target based on your weight, activity level, and goals.
How long does GLP-1-related hair shedding last?

Shedding often becomes noticeable two to three months after the triggering event and generally improves within a few months of correcting the underlying cause. Full regrowth and returning to previous fullness can take six months or longer.
When should I see a provider about hair loss during weight loss?

Reach out if hair loss is severe, keeps worsening, lasts beyond several months, occurs in patches, involves scalp irritation or scarring, or comes with other new symptoms. It may point to thyroid dysfunction, anemia, hormonal changes, or another condition that needs evaluation.
